As the population and industry soar, the CCP is under intense pressure to provide clean drinking water to Beijing and the rest of northern China.

China is one of the wettest nations on earth—in the south. The north, however, abuts the Gobi Desert all along the Mongolian border. CCP is desperate to bring in fresh sources of water. Multiple steps are being taken, such as [desalinating seawater](http://gizmodo.com/beijings-giant-new-desalination-plant-will-give-water-t-1564668242) as well as collaborating with Russia to [import water via aquaduct](https://voat.co/v/ModernPowers/comments/1056371).

But by far the biggest undertaking is the [South–North Water Transfer Project](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7s5UungzXhw), a series of canals designed to divert water over 1400 km from the [Yangtze River](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/5/51/Yangtze_River_Map.png) to the Yellow River and resevoirs of Bejiing and other northern cities. The first section of the Central Route was completed in 2014, after 12 years of construction. It is currently fed by water diverted from farmland until such time as the connection to the Yangtze can be completed.

But all this could be for naught if China doesn't get its pollution under control. More than 60% of groundwater wells are rated as "[unfit for human contact](https://www.rt.com/news/265186-china-water-air-pollution/)", and roughly 25% of surface water is [too polluted](http://www.reuters.com/article/us-china-environment-water-idUSTRE66P39H20100726) to be used in agriculture or even for industrial purposes.
